Graham was sworn in as interim senator last month following the death of her brother, Lindsey Graham; results also coming in from Vermont, Alabama and Connecticut

Defense Policy Board appointee Marc Andreessen’s firm, Andreessen Horowitz, one of Silicon Valley’s largest venture capital firms and known by the name “a16z”, co-invests alongside the Trump partnership 1789 Capital in three defense contractors. articles.author: Krishani Dhanji
articles.description:
The independent MP made the allegations in a letter to the National Anti-Corruption Commission. Follow today’s news live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Education minister says funding agreement with Victoria ‘very close’
The education minister, Jason Clare, says a funding deal with Victoria to get public schools funded to Gonski levels over the next decade is “very close”.
We’re very close, mate. I know [Victorian premier] Ben Carroll gets this, and I’m optimistic that we’ll get this across the line. He understands how important it is that teachers are paid well, that they do the best or do the most important job in the country, but how important it is that we fix the funding of our schools – we’ve struck agreements now, 10-year agreements, with every state and territory across the country except Victoria. We’re very close to landing that deal.
 Continue reading...

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Al-Ahmed, who maintains his innocence, was accused of putting his father in a headlock in March

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The man who disarmed one of the gunmen allegedly responsible for the Bondi beach terror attack has had an assault case against him tossed out.
Ahmed al-Ahmed, 44, had been accused of putting his father in a headlock on 9 March and intimidation over an alleged incident in June.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bondi shooting hero Ahmed al-Ahmed cleared of assault charges

articles.author: Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent
articles.description:
The Comac C919 will fly from Beijing to Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia, although experts say it could take generations for it to challenge the west’s dominance of the industry
China hopes to break into the world of commercial aviation with the first international flight of a Chinese-made passenger jet scheduled for Wednesday.
The Comac C919 will take off from Beijing capital international airport at 3pm, landing in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, just over two hours later.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Passenger jet billed as China’s answer to Boeing and Airbus prepares to make first international flight

articles.author: Dani Anguiano and agency
articles.description:
Nearly 500 personnel battle Timber fire in Los Padres national forest as blaze grows to 3,000 acres
Evacuations have been ordered for areas along California’s famous Big Sur coast as a wildfire burns in the nearby steep, rugged mountains.
The Timber fire in Monterey county started on Sunday and grew to nearly 3,000 acres by Tuesday evening, according to Cal Fire, the state’s fire agency. Nearly 500 fire personnel had been assigned to the fire in the Los Padres national forest.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Famed tourist destinations evacuated as wildfire threatens California’s Big Sur

articles.author: George Chidi
articles.description:
Norman beat out Russell Fry, a congressman, and Mark Sanford, a former governor, to advance is closely contested race

US politics live – latest updates

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

Senator Darline Graham, appointed to complete the Senate term of her late brother, Lindsey Graham of South Carolina will face congressman Ralph Norman in a runoff election for the Republican nomination.
Graham held a narrow lead in the polls going into the abbreviated special primary on Tuesday, which predicted a close contest for second place. Norman, Russell Fry, a congressman, and Mark Sanford, a former governor, had polled within a point of each other in the most recent survey from the Trafalgar Group.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Darline Graham to face Ralph Norman in South Carolina Republican primary runoff

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul calls  for tighter gun controls and ‘decisive penalties’ after nine dead in school shooting 
Thailand has suspended firearms licences after last week’s deadly school shooting, as the bodies of the teenage attacker and the grandparents he killed were cremated.
The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, said he had ordered the interior ministry and police to stop issuing licenses to possess, purchase and carry firearms, and called for “tighter controls and decisive penalties”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thailand suspends gun licences as teen shooter and grandparents he killed are cremated

articles.author: Kat Wong
articles.description:
Officers – correctly – may not have fully unzipped the bag containing the lifelike doll to avoid destroying evidence, one expert says

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Revelations that a “body” found inside a suitcase was actually a sex doll may have been embarrassing for police, but experts say officers followed the correct procedure.
New South Wales police on Sunday were called to Oallen, a town near Goulburn, after two members of the public found a suitcase containing what they believed to be human remains, dumped on the side of the road.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A ‘body’ found in a suitcase was actually a sex doll. How did NSW police get it so wrong?

articles.author: Joseph Gedeon and David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
Journalists and others were allowed to fly on presidential jet despite security threat while Trump was spirited away

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email 

Democrats called on Tuesday for a congressional briefing over a stunning charade in which Donald Trump was secretly spirited to a different plane than the one the public and press believed he was travelling on. Critics now question why reporters and the public had been deliberately misled.
When US intelligence allegedly found a credible threat that Iran plotted to kill him last month, Trump left Air Force One in a catering truck, an episode first reported by the Washington Post and also by the New York Times. While the president was reportedly snuck out the side door of the plane, more than a hundred aides, officials and reporters were kept onboard to fly towards Britain, without being told there was a threat to their lives.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s Air Force One deception faces scrutiny over ‘decoy’ passengers

articles.author: Rashneel Kumar in Rarotonga
articles.description:
The prime minister tells the Guardian that last year’s diplomatic rift with ally New Zealand could be on voters’ minds as they head to the polls
As voters in the Cook Islands prepare to head to the polls in a high-stakes general election, they will have much to reflect on. Over recent years, politics in this small island nation has been defined by fierce debates about deep-sea mining, diplomatic rifts with ally New Zealand and a major reshaping of the country’s foreign partnerships.
In an exclusive interview with the Guardian, days before Wednesday’s poll, Cook Islands prime minister Mark Brown defended his four-year term and the decisions he made that have seen this South Pacific nation of 17,000 people pushed into the international limelight, turning it into a battleground for influence between Beijing and western powers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cook Islands election: PM Mark Brown speaks on the diplomatic crises that defined his year

articles.author: Donna Lu
articles.description:
New research sheds light on the genetic basis of the venomous arachnid’s ‘weird mating behaviour’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

If you think you’ve had a bad one-night stand, spare a thought for the male redback spider, whose sole reproductive partner eats him after sex.
Male redbacks appear to invite this cannibalism through a “self-sacrificial somersault”, with new research shedding light on the genetic basis of the behaviour.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Male redback spiders invite cannibalism through a ‘self-sacrificial somersault’ during sex – but why?

articles.author: Maanvi Singh and agencies
articles.description:
According to manufacturer,  shock ‘is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds’
ICE plans to spend up to $20m (£15m) to purchase thousands of gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.
The devices, called Glove (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ICE to spend up to $20m on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks

articles.author: Peter Walker, Rajeev Syal and Caroline Davies
articles.description:
Letter signed by every chief constable in England and Wales warns freeing pair could weaken trust in justice system
Andy Burnham is facing an unprecedented mass call from police chiefs to block the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers, as unions warned his emergency plan to create more space in jails risked causing confusion or leading to prisoners being freed by mistake.
A letter signed by 50 police leaders across the UK, including every chief constable in England and Wales, called on the prime minister to do everything in his power to stop the killers benefiting from a programme designed to free up prison space, saying there was “a profound strength of feeling across policing” that this should not happen.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burnham urged by 50 police leaders to prevent early release of PC Harper’s killers

articles.author: Guardian staff
articles.description:
Reform deputy leader condemned for seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal reporter’s sources
Reform’s deputy leader Richard Tice has been accused of using “nasty tactics” in an attempt to intimidate journalists and deflect attention from his own financial affairs after issuing a legal threat to the Guardian.
In a letter sent from his lawyers, a Guardian correspondent was singled out for her reporting on a series of Tice’s financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Richard Tice accused of ‘nasty tactics’ over legal threat to the Guardian

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Star, 53, says disease has metastasised to her bones and it is too late for chemotherapy
Lucy Davis, the actor best known for playing Dawn Tinsley in The Office, has said she has incurable stage four breast cancer.
The 53-year-old said she was diagnosed a year and a half ago and the disease had metastasised to her bones including her spine, right hip and ribs. She said it was too late for chemotherapy.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Office actor Lucy Davis says she has incurable stage four breast cancer

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph in car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines

The only person to break the sound barrier in a car earned another world record on Tuesday in a show of force for hydrogen power.
British driver Andy Green reached 406.320mph (653.908km/h) in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, setting the record for that vehicle category, according to the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Driver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record in hydrogen-powered car

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Clifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’
A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP Stella Creasy after he was “abusive and aggressive” to her on a tube train.
Clifford Wilby, of east London, saw the MP for Walthamstow in July 2025 on a Victoria Line train, Westminster magistrates court heard.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Abusive’ man found guilty of harassing Stella Creasy MP on tube train

articles.description:
The new president is a former judge on the European Court of Human Rights
Spanish foreign minister José Manuel Albares visited Ceuta earlier today, as he insisted that Madrid had it all under control despite “the most unique and complex” border arrangements there.
He said Spain was in direct dialogue with the Moroccan authorities on how to prevent another border crisis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Former judge Baka elected new Hungarian president in another break from Orbán era – as it happened

articles.author: Alice Speri
articles.description:
Lawsuit challenges executive order targeting international criminal court for investigating Israeli crimes in Palestine
Four prominent US human rights organizations have accused the Trump administration of using its “crippling” sanctions regime against the international criminal court (ICC) to undermine global efforts to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity.
In a lawsuit filed in federal court on Tuesday, the groups – the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch and the Open Society Institute – argued that the administration’s targeting of the ICC, as well as of groups and individuals affiliated with it or assisting its work, amounts to a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice”, the groups said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Human rights groups sue Trump administration over ‘crippling’ ICC sanctions

articles.author: Patrick Commins Economics editor
articles.description:
When it comes to the Reserve Bank, there’s a whiff of a parent making a threat they have no intention of carrying out

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Every parent makes threats in an effort to get their kids to behave – and every parent hopes they won’t have to follow through.
Some (most?) parents even make threats they have zero intention of carrying out.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The RBA likely believes it won’t need to hike rates again – but the worst thing it could do is say that out loud

articles.author: Olivia Bowden in Toronto
articles.description:
Flight from Victoria to Toronto forced to return to terminal after repeated attempts to secure child in seat failed
A Canadian airline cancelled a flight from Victoria to Toronto after a child refused to wear a seatbelt.
The child was standing in their chair as the 6 August Porter Airlines flight taxied towards the runway, the airline said. Repeated attempts by an accompanying parent and crew to secure the child in their seat failed, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark as “the aircraft could not take off in this unsafe condition”, it added.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Canadian airline cancels flight after child refuses to wear seatbelt

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff
articles.description:
Rooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookings

Europe’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see it

Hotel prices have surged in key European cities as hundreds of thousands of tourists flock to see the first total eclipse visible from the continent this century.
Iceland’s capital, Reykjavík, has seen one of the biggest jumps in hotel room prices, being one of the few accessible locations to see the full eclipse before evening on Wednesday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse

articles.author: William Christou in Beirut
articles.description:
Verdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people died
A Syrian court has sentenced the country’s former president Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia for crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 14-year civil war, in which about half a million people died.
The two men fled to Moscow after being ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the dictatorial regime in just 11 days.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes

articles.author: Tom Phillips, and Thomas Graham in Bogotá
articles.description:
Quake of 7.4 magnitude collapses and severely damages buildings in several major cities, including Cali and Pereira
More than 100 people died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira.
The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was felt in neighbouring Venezuela, still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Scores dead in Colombia after powerful earthquake strikes west of country

articles.author: Patrick Greenfield
articles.description:
The wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 years
On 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release, Kazakhstan became the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.
Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The return of the caspian tiger: how a species feared extinct has come back to Kazakhstan

articles.author: Gwyn Topham and agencies
articles.description:
Air transport hub in west London reports 7.86m passengers in July, compared with 8.15m for Istanbul’s new airport away from the city

Istanbul airport has overtaken Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by passenger numbers, leading the London hub to say its “case for expansion has never been clearer”.
Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Flexible short-term bookings used to store and pack drugs and stash weapons and cash, says Ine Van Wymersch
Airbnb-type short-term rentals are being used as stash houses by criminal gangs for money, drugs, weapons and people, Belgium’s lead official in charge of countering drugs has said.
The booming e-commerce sector is helping “enormously” to facilitate organised crime, Belgium’s national drug commissioner, Ine Van Wymersch, said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Gangs using Airbnb-type rentals as drug stash houses, top Belgian official says

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
An Amnesty International report reveals that the country is now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. Plus, Assam floods, student anger spreads and a song to put in rotation
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
Hello, and welcome back to This Is India.
For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: As conflict in the Middle East intensifies, India’s relationship with Israel deepens

articles.author: Coral Murphy Marcos and agencies
articles.description:
Elaborate ruse was used to transport president to military flight from Air Force One in July
Donald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Turkey to Britain last month when the White House said he was flying aboard ⁠Air Force One, in an extraordinary ruse – prompted by an Iranian assassination threat – that involved hiding the president in an airport catering container, according to reporting from the Washington Post and the New York Times.
The operation took place when Trump was in Ankara for a Nato summit with world leaders, according to the Post. The president reportedly boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras, and then was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight, a US official told the Post.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump reportedly hid in catering container to board secret flight in Turkey amid Iran threat

articles.author: Adam Fulton, Lucy Campbell, Angus Thomson and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This blog is now closed – a full report is here
People remain trapped in Cali, one of Colombia’s largest cities, ​after more than two dozen structures ‌collapsed, mayor Alejandro Eder said. ‌
He added that the city had asked authorities in Bogota and Medellin to send disaster teams ‌to support rescue efforts.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Colombia quake leaves more than 110 dead – as it happened

articles.author: Andrew Roth in Washington
articles.description:
US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled
Donald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse.
The US president is trying to end conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths

articles.author: Penelope MacRae in Delhi
articles.description:
Demonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobs
Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.
Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police use teargas on young Indians as government jobs protest escalates

articles.author: Luke Harding and agencies
articles.description:
Attack hundreds of miles from border would be among deadliest of war as Kyiv aims to strangle Russian economy

A Ukrainian drone strike on an industrial city deep inside Russia has killed at least 13 people, according to the local mayor, as Kyiv steps up its campaign of long-range strikes on targets far from the frontline.
Kyiv said it hit the Taneco refinery in the city of Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles (1,200km) from the Ukrainian border. Footage circulating online appeared to show smoke rising from the refinery.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13

articles.author: José Olivares
articles.description:
Gabar Choli tells of how, for months, he was shackled, pinned and forcibly fed – and the physical and emotional scars the ordeal has left
In June 2025, a sluggish and thin Gabar Choli, with sunken temples and bones visible under his skin, braced himself for the immigration detention center guards to charge into his cell once again.
Choli was in a solitary confinement medical cell inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in south Texas where immigrants arrested in Donald Trump’s anti-immigration crackdown are detained.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Shoved the tube so hard it tore my nose’: Kurdish film-maker recounts ‘inhumane’ ICE force-feeding

articles.author: José Olivares in New York
articles.description:
Exclusive: Film-maker Gabar Choli describes how he endured coercive treatment over eight months in detention in Texas
A Kurdish man who was force-fed over the course of eight months while on hunger strike in US immigration detention has spoken out about it for the first time, describing how much the process harmed him physically and psychologically.
Gabar Choli, a film-maker and activist now living in Canada after being deported, described how he endured the coercive treatment – a practice widely considered torture by international human rights groups – often twice a day after being detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) when his asylum application was denied.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kurdish hunger striker says ICE force-feeding ‘mentally broke me’

articles.author: Magdalena Shopova for MetDesk
articles.description:
Drought and wildfires intensify across continent, while tropical storms bring heavy rain and disruption to east Asia
High pressure has dominated central and eastern Europe in early August, breaking temperature records  across the region. Austria recorded a high of 41.2C (106.2F), while Slovakia reached 42.2C. Hungary hit a peak of 41.8C, surpassing a record set in 1905, while overnight temperatures remained above 28C in some areas, marking it as a tropical night.
The extreme temperatures have been driven by a heat dome beneath the high-pressure system, which traps warm air close to the surface.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Weather tracker: Europe breaks more heat records as temperatures soar

articles.author: Shivam Patel
articles.description:
Mohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough killed during clashes between authorities and protesters
A British national was shot dead in Pakistan-administered Kashmir during clashes between security forces and protesters, the Guardian can reveal.
Another Briton has been held in a regional prison for more than two months despite his family’s efforts to secure his release through the Foreign Office.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British national shot dead in Kashmir by Pakistani security forces

articles.author: Yu-chen Li in Taipei
articles.description:
Authorities warn that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides as storm moves north and further inland
More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.
Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved from high-risk areas.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Typhoon Dolphin: more than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta
Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.
The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy

articles.author: Maya Yang and agency
articles.description:
Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians
Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.
On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections

articles.author: Kat Lay Global health correspondent
articles.description:
Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation
The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.
Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say

articles.author: Robert Tait in Washington
articles.description:
State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.
The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum

articles.author: Redwan Ahmed in Dhaka and Penelope MacRae in Delhi
articles.description:
Dhaka accuses India of giving platform to a ‘convicted genocider’ by allowing Sheikh Hasina to address journalists
Bangladesh has lashed out at India for allowing the ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina to address journalists in New Delhi, plunging already strained bilateral relations to a fresh low.
Dhaka accused India of giving a platform to a fugitive it labelled a “convicted genocider” and of undermining efforts to repair ties, after Hasina vowed to return to Bangladesh in December despite facing a death sentence on charges of “crimes against humanity”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India-Bangladesh relations hit new low over exiled PM’s speech to press in Delhi

articles.author: Carlos Mureithi
articles.description:
David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone
The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.
David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones

articles.author: Agence France-Press in Mumbai
articles.description:
Tarun Tejpal, ex-editor of Tehelka magazine, was initially acquitted in 2021 in case that drew nationwide attention
An Indian court has sentenced a high-profile former editor of an investigative news magazine to 10 years in prison after convicting him of raping a junior colleague, overturning his acquittal in a case that drew nationwide attention.
Tarun Tejpal, 63, the founder and former editor of Tehelka magazine, was accused of raping a journalist in the lift of a five-star hotel in the western coastal state of Goa during an event in November 2013. He was arrested and spent seven months in jail until the supreme court granted him bail.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: High-profile Indian journalist jailed for 10 years for raping colleague

articles.author: George Chidi
articles.description:
Norman beat out Russell Fry, a congressman, and Mark Sanford, a former governor, to advance is closely contested race

US politics live – latest updates

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

Senator Darline Graham, appointed to complete the Senate term of her late brother, Lindsey Graham of South Carolina will face congressman Ralph Norman in a runoff election for the Republican nomination.
Graham held a narrow lead in the polls going into the abbreviated special primary on Tuesday, which predicted a close contest for second place. Norman, Russell Fry, a congressman, and Mark Sanford, a former governor, had polled within a point of each other in the most recent survey from the Trafalgar Group.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Darline Graham to face Ralph Norman in South Carolina Republican primary runoff

articles.author: Joseph Gedeon and David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
Journalists and others were allowed to fly on presidential jet despite security threat while Trump was spirited away

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email 

Democrats called on Tuesday for a congressional briefing over a stunning charade in which Donald Trump was secretly spirited to a different plane than the one the public and press believed he was travelling on. Critics now question why reporters and the public had been deliberately misled.
When US intelligence allegedly found a credible threat that Iran plotted to kill him last month, Trump left Air Force One in a catering truck, an episode first reported by the Washington Post and also by the New York Times. While the president was reportedly snuck out the side door of the plane, more than a hundred aides, officials and reporters were kept onboard to fly towards Britain, without being told there was a threat to their lives.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s Air Force One deception faces scrutiny over ‘decoy’ passengers

articles.author: Maanvi Singh and agencies
articles.description:
According to manufacturer,  shock ‘is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds’
ICE plans to spend up to $20m (£15m) to purchase thousands of gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.
The devices, called Glove (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ICE to spend up to $20m on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Ruling expands on earlier order that prevented implementation in 23 mostly Democratic-led states

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

A federal judge on Tuesday blocked ⁠the US Postal ⁠Service ​(USPS) from implementing part of Donald Trump’s executive order that aims ⁠to tighten rules for mail-in voting ahead of November midterm elections that ⁠will decide control of Congress.
The ruling by ​US district ‌judge Indira ‌Talwani in Boston in effect expanded on an ‌earlier order she had issued in June that had prevented Trump’s administration from implementing it in 23 mostly Democratic-led states.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Judge blocks Trump’s order aimed at using USPS to restrict mail-in voting

articles.author: Lucy Campbell and agency
articles.description:
Group says new executive order is attempt to evade supreme court’s earlier ruling against the president

US politics live – latest updates

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and other advocacy groups have asked a federal judge to block Donald Trump from enforcing new executive ⁠orders he signed last week in his latest attempt to restrict eligibility ​for birthright citizenship in the US.
In a Tuesday court filing, the groups called the US president’s new orders an improper attempt to evade the US supreme court’s 30 June rejection of his first, more sweeping bid to deny automatic citizenship to children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary foreign residents.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ACLU asks judge to block new Trump order restricting birthright citizenship

articles.author: Editorial
articles.description:
Amid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome development
As the huge societal ramifications of artificial intelligence have become clear, some of the tech industry’s most senior figures have taken to writing thinkpieces on what comes next. The latest to do so is Mark Zuckerberg, who this week published 6,500 words making the case for a laissez-faire approach to AI development. Worrying too much about regulation, Meta’s CEO unsurprisingly opines, could lead to the United States falling behind in the race to own the future.
Mr Zuckerberg’s plea for maximum autonomy is, of course, self-serving. Much of his essay – which airily envisions “invention superpowers” for every entrepreneur and “an abundance of jobs in the future” – reads like unadulterated tech-utopianism. But the lobbying at least has the merit of being out there in the open. As midterm elections loom in the US, darker arts are also being used to counter popular concern about what AI will mean for a host of topics, from the labour market to child safety, the environment and cybersecurity.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | Editorial

articles.author: Francine Prose
articles.description:
Our children should be able to visit our nation’s capital without having to think about Donald Trump and about how much he did to deface it
History has shown us how much dictators and aspiring dictators love building monuments to themselves. They enjoy reminding the world that they can do anything, no matter who is responsible for the physical labor or who will be paying the financial and human cost.
They prefer outsized structures, heroic arches, towers and columns designed to prove that their signature and their esthetic will be with us forever, even after they’re dead, though dictators often seem to believe they are too powerful to die.
Francine Prose is a former president of PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump put a wrecking-ball through the East Wing – and through democratic norms | Francine Prose

articles.author: Hosted by Carter Sherman , produced by Anabel Bacon , engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Jonathan Menjivar
articles.description:
Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan may soon be extradited back to the UK – but the manosphere influencers' case will have lasting consequences in the US, where the Tates reportedly maintained multiple ties to the Trump administration. (The Tates have been charged with rape, trafficking and numerous other crimes, but deny all criminal wrongdoing.) Host Carter Sherman talks with author and Guardian columnist Rebecca Solnit about what the Andrew Tate saga reveals about Republicans' approach toward sexual violence and Donald Trump's connections to the manosphere. They ask: do people secretly like it when the US president hates women?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rebecca Solnit on Andrew Tate and Trump’s misogyny – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Rachel Leingang in Milwaukee, Wisconsin
articles.description:
Hong, whose grassroots campaign has made her a frontrunner, aims for primary win after public skepticism from top Democrats and a last-minute shake-up
As Francesca Hong surged ahead in the final weeks of the chaotic Democratic primary to be Wisconsin’s next governor, the democratic socialist has become the internet’s main character.
Donald Trump has mocked her old tweets, while major figures in her own party publicly questioned her ability to win a general election. The man she is vying to succeed even launched a late blitz in support of one of her rivals.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Will democratic socialist Francesca Hong shake up the establishment – or help Republicans win Wisconsin?

articles.author: José Olivares
articles.description:
Gabar Choli tells of how, for months, he was shackled, pinned and forcibly fed – and the physical and emotional scars the ordeal has left
In June 2025, a sluggish and thin Gabar Choli, with sunken temples and bones visible under his skin, braced himself for the immigration detention center guards to charge into his cell once again.
Choli was in a solitary confinement medical cell inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in south Texas where immigrants arrested in Donald Trump’s anti-immigration crackdown are detained.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Shoved the tube so hard it tore my nose’: Kurdish film-maker recounts ‘inhumane’ ICE force-feeding

articles.author: Margaret Sullivan
articles.description:
It’s easy to second-guess decisions made during the pandemic. That doesn’t justify the Republicans’ politicized response
Like the rest of us, Anthony Fauci is far from perfect. His influential guidance, as the country’s top infectious-disease specialist during the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, certainly didn’t get everything right.
A great deal about the deadly disease – where it came from, how it spread, how best to protect the public – was unknown, or was being learned midstream, during a crisis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Dr Fauci made mistakes. But his persecution is a travesty | Margaret Sullivan

articles.author: Nesrine Malik
articles.description:
Americans want someone on their side in the fight against vested interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran Mamdani
Abdul El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Senate primary was a historic breakthrough. Not only because he is a Muslim son of immigrants who broke with almost every single tenet of establishment Democratic party politics. But because he has wiped that complacent sneer at progressive wins off the faces of centrist gatekeepers. Zohran Mamdani? Relax, he’s just a mayor. And it’s New York City. Outside urban and liberal corridors, there is nothing to worry about. Now El-Sayed has won the Democratic party’s nomination in a swing state that is also on the list of presidential nomination states.
There is a lot to be excited about. Not only within the US, but for observers abroad hopeful for the emergence of a truly revolutionary left that is able to weather powerful and well-funded adversaries and prevail. The money raised to defeat El-Sayed was staggering. He was outspent by more than nine to one. It was the most expensive Democratic congressional primary ever. A roll call of cartoon bad guys, such as Chevron and Philip Morris, funded his opponent, Haley Stevens, to the tune of over $60m. Of that funding, nearly half came from a Super Pac backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Centrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not? | Nesrine Malik

articles.author: Edward Helmore
articles.description:
Jurors hear from host of medical experts as defence says postpartum psychosis caused young mother to kill children
It’s been called “America’s saddest murder trial” and last week jurors in the Lindsay Clancy case listened to mental health professionals, counsellors, psychiatrists and medication experts explain the circumstances in which the young mother killed her three children.
It has been a spectacle that has gripped America, not least because Clancy’s legal defense has been supported by her now divorced husband.
In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. You can also reach Crisis Text Line by texting MHA to 741741. In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘America’s saddest murder trial’: mental health in focus in Lindsay Clancy case

articles.author: David Smith
articles.description:
With Abdul El-Sayed’s win, the party’s leftwing insurgency had breached the walls of a midwestern swing state, forcing a reckoning about Democrats’ direction and leadership
Standing before The Spirit of Detroit, a landmark bronze statue in the city’s downtown, in the early hours of a Wednesday morning, Abdul El-Sayed channelled boxing great Muhammad Ali. “We shook up the world,” he declared.
The 41-year-old former public health official had just delivered a knockout blow to the Democratic establishment, defeating the US congresswoman Haley Stevens to claim the party’s nomination for the Senate in swing state Michigan.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Voters are fed up’: Michigan primary forces Democratic party to accept leftwing shift

articles.author: Presented by Jonathan Freedland, produced by May Robson and Nada Smiljanic . The executive producers were Maz Ebtehaj and Danielle Stephens
articles.description:
Donald Trump’s second term is unlike his first. The politicians who challenged him are gone. The lawyers who once pushed back now choose their battles. What remains is an imperial president with almost no internal checks - using executive power to reshape everything from the economy to immigration and even the presidency itself.

Few journalists have covered Trump as closely as the New York Times's Jonathan Swan. He speaks to Jonathan Freedland about how the president has consolidated such enormous power and what it could mean for America - and the world.

Regime Change by Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman https://guardianbookshop.com/regime-change-9781398567597/
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump unbound: the making of an imperial presidency | Politics Weekly America

articles.author: Rachel Leingang Hazel Tang John Farrell
articles.description:
Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, beat Haley Stevens to win the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan. El-Sayed will now face Republican Mike Rogers in November. Here are three major takeaways of the race from the Guardian's midwest politics correspondent Rachel Leingang
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three key takeaways from Michigan's Democratic Senate primary – video explainer

articles.author: Hosted by Carter Sherman , produced by Tiara Chiaramonte , engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producers Jonathan Menjivar and Rachel Humphreys
articles.description:
Democrats are pissed off – and they're taking their anger straight to the ballot box. In the wake of Donald Trump's return to the White House, progressives (including members of DSA – Democratic Socialists of America) have defeated established moderates in elections in liberal cities like New York, Washington DC and Seattle. Now, they're trying to win a series of major primaries in the deep-purple midwest. Host Carter Sherman speaks with Guardian midwest political correspondent Rachel Leingang, who has traveled all over the region covering several key races – including this week's Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, where progressive Abdul Al-Sayed is squaring off against the establishment candidate, Haley Stevens. Can leftist politics win outside of blue bubbles? And what do these races reveal about the fight for the midterms and the White House?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mamdani won New York. Can a progressive win the Michigan primary? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Peter Walker, Rajeev Syal and Caroline Davies
articles.description:
Letter signed by every chief constable in England and Wales warns freeing pair could weaken trust in justice system
Andy Burnham is facing an unprecedented mass call from police chiefs to block the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers, as unions warned his emergency plan to create more space in jails risked causing confusion or leading to prisoners being freed by mistake.
A letter signed by 50 police leaders across the UK, including every chief constable in England and Wales, called on the prime minister to do everything in his power to stop the killers benefiting from a programme designed to free up prison space, saying there was “a profound strength of feeling across policing” that this should not happen.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burnham urged by 50 police leaders to prevent early release of PC Harper’s killers

articles.author: Guardian staff
articles.description:
Reform deputy leader condemned for seeking disclosure of documents that could reveal reporter’s sources
Reform’s deputy leader Richard Tice has been accused of using “nasty tactics” in an attempt to intimidate journalists and deflect attention from his own financial affairs after issuing a legal threat to the Guardian.
In a letter sent from his lawyers, a Guardian correspondent was singled out for her reporting on a series of Tice’s financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Richard Tice accused of ‘nasty tactics’ over legal threat to the Guardian

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
The PM is proposing three ways of increasing jail capacity – but none offer a quick or straightforward solution
Andy Burnham said on Monday he was “increasingly confident” that PC Andrew Harper’s killers would not be freed in the new year.
Determined to ensure that Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter, serve their full sentences, he has asked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to examine three options for increasing prison capacity.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How viable are plans to free up prison space in England and Wales?

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Star, 53, says disease has metastasised to her bones and it is too late for chemotherapy
Lucy Davis, the actor best known for playing Dawn Tinsley in The Office, has said she has incurable stage four breast cancer.
The 53-year-old said she was diagnosed a year and a half ago and the disease had metastasised to her bones including her spine, right hip and ribs. She said it was too late for chemotherapy.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Office actor Lucy Davis says she has incurable stage four breast cancer

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
British driver Andy Green reached 406.320 mph in car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines

The only person to break the sound barrier in a car earned another world record on Tuesday in a show of force for hydrogen power.
British driver Andy Green reached 406.320mph (653.908km/h) in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, setting the record for that vehicle category, according to the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Driver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record in hydrogen-powered car

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Clifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’
A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP Stella Creasy after he was “abusive and aggressive” to her on a tube train.
Clifford Wilby, of east London, saw the MP for Walthamstow in July 2025 on a Victoria Line train, Westminster magistrates court heard.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Abusive’ man found guilty of harassing Stella Creasy MP on tube train

articles.author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
articles.description:
The prime minister’s money-saving policies are popular but they are yet to convince voters he can take on the big things
It was last year that Martin Lewis, the money-saving guru, advised the government to find “100 small things that piss people off” and set about sorting them out.
That approach has been adopted almost immediately by Andy Burnham since entering office, as he began his programme of “everyday fixes” to tackle problems that can be dealt with through minor policy tweaks.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

articles.author: Tom Ambrose (now); Martin Belam and Yohannes Lowe (earlier)
articles.description:
Prediction comes amid warning of ‘extreme heat’ this week with temperatures of 38C possible
The Guardian’s environment editor, Fiona Harvey, has written a useful explainer about the UK public services that are struggling in the extreme weather. You can read it in full here:
There’s only one solution in the end to the drought now declared across most of England and that’s rain, says Hannah Cloke, professor of hydrology at the University of Reading.
An important consequence of drought is that very dry soils can become less able to absorb rainfall when it does arrive. This can increase surface runoff and can even contribute to localised flash flooding, particularly if rain falls intensely over a short period.
The current situation highlights the need to improve long-term resilience to both drought and flood risk as climate variability increases, and shows one more damaging impact of the burning of fossil fuels.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Summer 2026 on course to be UK’s hottest on record, says Met Office – as it happened

articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.description:
Union chief says vote is about staff ‘warning they cannot protect the public properly’
In his pooled TV interview, Andy Burnham repeated the point he made in his Facebook post earlier (see 9.58am), saying he was confident that more could be done to free up space in the prison system (which would allow the early release system to be changed so that PC Andrew Harper’s killers are excluded). Burnham said that since becoming PM he had been pushing the system “every single day” to go further.
Explaining how extra space could be found (see 9.19am), he particularly singled out the more than 2,000 prisoners on indeterminate IPP (imprisonment for public protection) sentences. He said:
[The] plan will include issues like returning more foreign national offenders to their country of origin, and looking at the injustice of IPP sentences, which have led to young people, or young when they were imprisoned, being imprisoned indeterminately, and that clearly is unfair.
My office was in touch with the family last night [see 10.04am], and I know the justice secretary is in regular touch as well.
So, we will keep close to the family through this whole process because we understand how difficult this process has been for them.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Probation officers vote for strike action after warning early releases will add to excessive workloads - as it happened

articles.author: Sandra Laville in the New Forest
articles.description:
Key tourist route closed and residents rallying round as battle against wildfire expected to go on for several days
The battle to contain a large wildfire spreading across the New Forest will go on for several days, experts have said, as wind changes and a desiccated landscape fuel the flames.
Smoke billowed above the deserted A31 road, the main tourist route into the New Forest national park where tens of thousands of families are on holiday, late on Tuesday while a helicopter flew above the blaze. Firefighters at the scene said they were trying to contain several hotspots across the more than 100 hectares (247 acres) of dried heathland as winds swirled over the area.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Real struggle’ to tame New Forest blaze as UK set for hottest summer on record

articles.author: Daisy Ayliffe
articles.description:
Prof Wyn Evans, who raised concerns over treatment of female staff at Institute of Astronomy, was subject to ‘baseless’ investigation, judge rules
A University of Cambridge whistleblower who alleged bullying of female staff inside the university’s Institute of Astronomy has won a tribunal against his employer.
Prof Wyn Evans told a tribunal hearing in June that the institute suffered from “a bad history of misogyny”. He claimed that one woman in the department had been “hounded out of a job”, another was “left a frightened woman”, and a third had faced “aggressive professors” at the institute.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: University of Cambridge whistleblower who reported alleged bullying wins employment tribunal

articles.author: Phillip Inman
articles.description:
The new PM could bring in revenue for social care or defence with a land levy or by reforming council tax
Residential property is the largest store of wealth in the UK, and has long been a target for those who believe homes should be taxed more. Real estate remains a juicy plum for Andy Burnham to pick as he searches for ways to pay for an overhaul of the social care system and higher defence spending, to name just two fiscal priorities. Yet how to tax property, or possibly the land it sits on, has vexed economists and politicians for centuries. Here we discuss the background to the debate and some of the tax options.
• This article was amended on 11 August 2026. An earlier version said home occupiers in France must pay the taxe d’habitation; in fact, since 2023 this only applies to second homes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Axe stamp duty? How Andy Burnham could change property tax

articles.author: Alexandra Topping Political correspondent
articles.description:
Poll finds consensus on what makes people proud to be British but deep divisions on issues such as immigration
You may think it’s a commitment to buying a round, the ability to chat at length about the weather, or making a proper cup of tea. But when it comes down to what makes people proud to be British, there is a consensus across all ages, demographics and political groups – and tea, pints and the weather don’t get a look-in.
Hard work, fair play and community are the values that voters – no matter which political party, age group, social class or region they come from – instinctively believe capture what it means to be British, according to a large-scale study of British values by Public First.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hard work or humour? Take the British values quiz

articles.author: Peter Walker and Caroline Davies
articles.description:
Prime minister says he has asked justice secretary to push through measures to increase the number of prison places
Andy Burnham has said he is increasingly confident he can adapt the early release scheme for prisoners to exclude the killers of PC Andrew Harper and other serious offenders, saying he understood and shared the public’s concern about their potential release.
Writing on Facebook, the prime minister said on Tuesday he had asked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to rapidly push through a series of measures to increase the number of prison places, requiring fewer people to be released early to free up room.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burnham ‘increasingly confident’ PC Harper’s killers will not get early release

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff
articles.description:
Rooms in Icelandic capital Reykjavík cost double usual rate and Spain also enjoying strong bookings

Europe’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see it

Hotel prices have surged in key European cities as hundreds of thousands of tourists flock to see the first total eclipse visible from the continent this century.
Iceland’s capital, Reykjavík, has seen one of the biggest jumps in hotel room prices, being one of the few accessible locations to see the full eclipse before evening on Wednesday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse

articles.author: Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent
articles.description:
After widespread outcry, PM is confident he can adapt scheme to exclude Harper’s killers but his options are limited

Andy Burnham is said to be exploring “every option” to block the early release from prison of the killers of PC Andrew Harper under plans to alleviate the prison overcrowding crisis, amid public concern that they could be back on the streets next year. As he faces what many are calling his first big test since becoming prime minister, what are his options?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What could Andy Burnham do to block early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers?

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Charity says government must focus on securing housing for ex-prisoners if Burnham is to meet rough-sleeping promise

Andy Burnham’s pledge to end rough sleeping in England is under threat from a failure to find accommodation for a growing number of newly released prisoners, a charity has said.
An analysis by the social justice charity Nacro has found that nearly one in six people leaving jail in England and Wales last year were released into homelessness, reaching the highest rate for five years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Early prisoner releases mean pledge to cut rough sleeping ‘may fail’

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff and agency
articles.description:
Apollo, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and KKR among those working with chipmaker to fund infrastructure
Nvidia ⁠has struck a deal with six large Wall Street firms to raise ⁠more than $500bn (£370bn) to fund the datacentres, chip factories and power stations needed to fuel the artificial intelligence boom.
The Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, said on X that it marked “a major milestone for Nvidia and the AI industry”, as he posted a photo of himself smiling and giving a thumbs up alongside finance bosses involved in the deal, including the head of Goldman Sachs, David Solomon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nvidia links with Wall Street firms for $500bn AI financing deal

articles.author: Gwyn Topham and agencies
articles.description:
Air transport hub in west London reports 7.86m passengers in July, compared with 8.15m for Istanbul’s new airport away from the city

Istanbul airport has overtaken Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by passenger numbers, leading the London hub to say its “case for expansion has never been clearer”.
Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport

articles.author: Pippa Neill and Safeerah Ahmed
articles.description:
Last month in England was the driest July since records began almost two centuries ago. How concerned should we be?
Almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales are now officially in drought. But what does this mean and could taps eventually run dry?
• The headline of this article was amended on 7 August 2026 to refer to England and Wales, rather than the UK. Also, the average usage of 139 litres of water a day is for people in England and Wales, not in the UK as stated in an earlier version; and the 47bn kilolitres of water extracted from the environment in 2023 was in England only. Groundwater was added to the list of main sources of water.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Could England and Wales ever run out of water?

articles.author: Michael Segalov
articles.description:
In today’s newsletter: As we enter our fifth summer heatwave, Andy Burnham’s government is looking at what the UK should do with its remaining North Sea oil and gas
Good morning. What a difference a new job can make. “To have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can’t have any new oil or gasfields … It’s irresponsible and shortsighted to be funding new #fossilfuels when we need to be getting to #NetZero.”

 This was the 2022 message from Miatta Fahnbulleh, now the secretary of state for energy security and net zero. It’s a testament to her remarkable rise that Fahnbulleh wasn’t even an MP when she posted it four years ago. Today, she is in the cabinet, facing (or is the face of, at least) one of the most challenging, and potentially controversial questions looming for the new …
articles.title: Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test

articles.author: Caroline Davies, Matthew Pearce and Pippa Neill
articles.description:
Exclusive: FBU calls for more funding as ‘unprecedented summer’ puts rising demands on already stretched crews
Firefighters in the UK are under increased pressure as a result of an “unprecedented summer of dangerous and volatile wildfires”, the Fire Brigades Union has said, as many parts of the country brace for a fifth heatwave of the year.
As authorities declared almost three-quarters of England was now in drought, Steve Wright, the FBU general secretary, said the unpredictable environmental challenges the UK was now confronted with meant it was a “national priority” to have enough properly equipped firefighters to “face these threats”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘National priority’ to equip UK firefighters amid growing wildfire threat

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Four more regions given drought status, putting 27 million people under restrictions on water use
Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought, as much of Europe braces for its fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave this summer.
Four more regions of England have officially been declared to be in drought: the East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three-quarters of England in drought as summer’s fifth heatwave looms

articles.author: Daniel Boffey Chief reporter
articles.description:
Industry body says use of private investigators against reporters is ‘attack on our democracy’ after Banks apparently admitted doing so
The businessman and Reform UK backer Arron Banks is facing calls to lay out the extent of his surveillance of journalists, described by an industry body as an “attack on our democracy”.
The News Media Association (NMA), which represents regional and national media, raised concerns after Banks appeared to admit over the weekend to hiring private investigators to spy on a Sunday Times journalist.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Reform backer Arron Banks urged to set out extent of surveillance of journalists

articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.description:
A spokesperson for the human rights group likened the proposal to ‘financial brutality with British taxpayers’ money’
Farage and Yusuf are now taking questions.
Q: [From Jack Fenwick from the BBC] Are there other countries where you might send foreign offenders? And how much would this cost?
We have to admit that there might not be too many colour TVs.
It’s not going to be a summer camp. It’s not going to be particularly fun. But it won’t be cruel and it won’t be unreasonable.
We will rapidly build capacity. We will take advantage of new prefabricated modular technology and build 12,000 prison places in the form of Nightingale prisons on Ministry of Defence land. And the army will be called in to assist.
Together, these measures will create an additional 22,000 prison places compared to Andy Burnham’s plans.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Amnesty International says Farage putting ‘hate and inhumanity’ over leadership with El Salvador prison plan – as it happened

articles.author: Angus Thomson and PA Media
articles.description:
Fire crews racing to contain fire and protect fragile heathland habitat that is ‘rarer than rainforest’
Efforts to contain a “devastating” blaze in the New Forest will continue into a second night as firefighting crews race to protect the fragile heathland and rare species.
The area hit by the blaze, which started after a van caught fire on the A31 near Ringwood on Sunday, is protected heathland that is home to a number of rare species, according to the New Forest national park authority.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Firefighters spend second night battling ‘devastating’ New Forest blaze

articles.author: Steven Morris
articles.description:
Some online shoppers may have left it too late to order – but you can view partial eclipse indirectly without specs
A frantic rush is on across the UK to find the right kind of protective eyewear ahead of Wednesday’s partial solar eclipse.
High street stores are running out of eclipse glasses and online shoppers who track down a pair are being told they may not reach them until the end of the week. In other words, in plenty of time for the next comparable UK eclipse – in 2081 – but no good at all for Wednesday’s show.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rush to find solar eclipse glasses as UK high street stocks run short

articles.author: Jasper Jolly
articles.description:
Utility firm’s payment criticised by Defra and campaign groups, with some urging Andy Burnham to nationalise it

Nils Pratley: Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect?

Thames Water has paid its finance chief a £1m signing fee despite teetering on the brink of a government-handled administration – a decision the environment department labelled “unacceptable”.
The utility company revealed that it made the payment last month, in a letter sent last week by Adrian Montague, its chair, to MPs on the environment, food and rural affairs select committee.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thames Water’s £1m payout to finance chief is ‘unacceptable’, says government department

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Regulator acts after 12,000 complaints over comments by Caroline Farrow linking parades with bestiality and paedophilia
GB News is being investigated by the UK’s media regulator after a guest appeared to link pride parades with bestiality and paedophilia.
The remarks are thought to have set a new record for individual complaints about a GB News programme, with more than 12,000 people raising concerns about comments made by the guest Caroline Farrow.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ofcom investigates GB News over guest’s pride and paedophilia remarks

articles.author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey, produced by Frankie Tobi, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
In July, Andy Burnham told the Guardian’s political editor, Pippa Crerar, that Labour ‘didn’t get it right’ on Gaza. He apologised for the party’s slow response in calling for a ceasefire, but stopped short of describing what was happening on the ground as genocide.
This is an edited version of Pippa’s conversation with colleague Kiran Stacey. The original episode was published on 9 July
You can read Pippa Crerar’s exclusive with Andy Burnham here.
You can read Anna Isaac’s investigation into Nigel Farage and Reform UK here.
Please keep sending your comments and questions to Pippa and Kiran at politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com.
Please follow and subscribe to the Politics Weekly YouTube channel here.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Revisited: Andy Burnham apologises for Labour’s stance on Gaza – podcast

articles.author: Shane Hickey
articles.description:
Those tempted to access fake websites run risk of phishing scams and having computer infected with malware
The Odyssey is the hottest release this summer and you have been looking forward to seeing the much-acclaimed adaptation of Homer’s epic ancient Greek poem. But you have been unable to go to the cinema, so when you spot an ad to watch online, you jump at the chance.
There are positive reviews posted on the site so you decide to sign up. Although it asks for your bank details – which is unusual for a “free” trial – you are so eager to watch the blockbuster you input your details.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Watch The Odyssey for free online’: scam targets film fans with fake streaming sites

articles.author: Rachel Hall
articles.description:
When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this century
For the first time this century, people across the UK will be able to see an almost total solar eclipse in the evening sky on Wednesday.
A solar eclipse occurs when the moon moves between the sun and the Earth, blocking the sun’s light either partly or fully. This year, people in the UK and Ireland will see 90-96% of the sun covered by the moon for the first time since 1999 – and it’s their last chance until 2081.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?

articles.author: Hannah Al-Othman and Rory Carroll in Belfast
articles.description:
A horrific knife attack on a street in June sparked another summer’s night of racial violence, stoked by loyalist groups. How did the unrest erupt – and why do many fear it will happen again?
Shortly after 10.30pm on Monday 8 June, as a summer twilight lingered over Belfast, a horrific scene unfolded on Kinnaird Avenue: a man straddled and repeatedly stabbed a figure lying on the ground in a bloody assault that ended only after onlookers intervened.
Others captured the drama on cameraphones and uploaded the footage to social media. Once seen, the grainy images were hard to forget, and by dawn on Tuesday 9 June they were ricocheting around X, WhatsApp, Facebook, Telegram and other platforms.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The night Belfast burned: how the Northern Ireland race riots unfolded

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Industry body calls for more regular reviews of repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’
The amount of wasted medicines thrown away in England in one year could fill 75 swimming pools, according to a pharmacy group.
The National Pharmacy Association (NPA) estimated that 3,400 tonnes of partly used medicines were disposed of in England in 2024-25.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wasted medicine in England could fill 75 swimming pools a year, pharmacy group says

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
Exclusive: Seven in 10 survey respondents expect services to be reduced or shut, while more than half anticipate job losses
Millions of adults and children in England face being forced to wait longer for mental health care, with more than two-thirds of NHS providers planning to cut services and half expected to axe jobs, the Guardian can reveal.
With mental health services already under extraordinary pressure amid soaring demand for support, experts warned the proposed cuts – drawn up by trusts to plug holes in their finances – would also have “significant” consequences for the wider NHS, the economy and public services.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Millions in England face longer waits for mental health care as NHS providers plan cuts

articles.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
articles.description:
Experts say the attackers’ behaviour, and the handling of their cases, have striking similarities
• Simon Levy convicted of double murder while free on bail
About 40 metres off Tottenham High Street, up a slip road for deliveries to a B&M homewares store, is a stretch of concrete paving behind a 2-metre wall topped with spikes.
This is the patch of ground that Simon Levy tried to turn into his personal killing field.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Simon Levy murders: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing?

articles.author: Caroline Davies and Nadia Khomami
articles.description:
Festival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmate 
The Edinburgh festival fringe has said it is “not afraid of controversy” after it faced calls to cancel a sold-out show by Amanda Knox, who was wrongfully convicted for the 2007 murder of her flatmate Meredith Kercher in Italy.
Knox’s comedy show, Cartwheel, has been condemned by Kercher’s family, with her sister, Stephanie, saying it “normalises and trivialises violence against women”. A petition calling for it to be cancelled has been signed by more than 9,000 people.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd and Lanre Bakare, with Eli Block, Alex Atack, Nilufer Aumeerally and Brian McNamara; executive producer Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
Jason Arday’s appointment as Cambridge’s youngest black professor made global headlines. Then questions about his meteoric rise began to snowball. Lanre Bakare reports.
When the University of Cambridge appoints a new professor, it doesn’t usually make global headlines. But Jason Arday was different. He was just 37 in 2023 when he became Cambridge’s youngest black professor, specialising in the sociology of race and education. The achievement seemed all the more remarkable because of his incredible back story.
Born to Ghanaian parents who moved to the UK in the early 1980s, Arday was diagnosed with global development delay and autism spectrum disorder at three years of age. He said he hadn’t learned to speak until he was 11 and that he couldn’t really read and write until he was 18. But he defied all expectations, and as his star rose, he received honours usually reserved for celebrities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Plagiarism and a pig’s head: the rise and fall of Jason Arday – podcast

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Ben Quinn ; produced by Bryony Moore and Leonore Schick ; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin
articles.description:
